newsitem.title: USA: Calif. thermal power plants get "must-run" status.
newsitem.headline: Calif. thermal power plants get "must-run" status.

text.p: The governing board of California's independent transmission system operator (ISO) has designated as "must-run" most of the state's utility-owned thermal power plants, industry sources said.
The move limits the volume of power which will be open to competitive bidding when the state begins to deregulate its electricity industry on January 1.

"There is some tension here as we move forward between the need to assure reliability and the push for an open market," said Mark Ziering, manager of the California Public Utilities Commission's (CPUC) reliabilty project.

The decision was made last week after a consultant study indicated 90 percent of the state's power plants were "must-run" under a worst-case scenario of two failed nuclear plants and two other unit or line outages, one source noted.
The overall capacity of the thermal plants, which are mostly natural gas-fired, is estimated at 17,000 megawatts, or about a third of the state's total power generating capacity.

The plants were previously identified by their owners, PG&E Corp's Pacific Gas & Electric Co and Edison International's Southern California Edison Co, as key to the reliable operation of the state's electricity system.
As part of California's efforts to deregulate the power industry, PG&E and Edison were ordered to divest half of their fossil fuel-fired generating assets.
But both companies--eager to embrace their new role as mainly distribution utilities--have since decided to sell off nearly all of their California thermal power plants.
The newly-designated must-run units will retain that status no matter who owns them, sources familiar with the ISO decision said.
They noted, however, that final authority over this and other aspects of California's plans will rest with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in Washington.

As part of overall deregulation of the industry, California earlier decided to require investor-owned utilities (IOUs) to sell electricity from their nuclear and hydroelectric plants into the power exchange as of next year.

The addition of the thermal plants to these mandated sales volumes will mean less of the state's electricity demand will be open to competitive bidding once the Power Exchange (PX) is launched on January 1.
Ziering at the CPUC stressed the ISO will have authority as of January 1 to reassess the cost-based contracts with the power plant owners.

The utilities' hydro and nuclear resources total roughly 10,000 MW, although the hydropower portion of the total varies widely due to annual precipitation levels, according to the latest statistics from the CPUC.

The state's total generating capacity--including that of investor-owned utilities, public utilities and qualifying facilitites--totals around 51,000 MW, while power imports from the Pacific Northwest and desert Southwest supply the state with another 5,000 MW or so, the CPUC said.

In addition to the mandated PX sales--of hydro and nuclear power in the case of the IOU's and of thermal generation in the case of the eventual owners of the divested plants--an unknown volume of the state's demand will be met through bilateral contracts.
Under this option, large industrial buyers or aggregated groups of smaller consumers will contract with a supplier of their choice to buy power at fixed or indexed prices.
